findings.description: AWS access key ID and secret access key are hardcoded in plaintext in the EC2 user_data script, which is readable by anyone with DescribeInstanceAttribute permissions and visible in the instance metadata service.
The instance does not configure metadata_options to require IMDSv2 (http_tokens = required), leaving the legacy instance metadata service enabled and vulnerable to SSRF-based credential theft.
The EBS volume does not enable encryption (encrypted = true is commented out), so data at rest on this volume is stored unencrypted.
The EBS snapshot inherits the lack of encryption from the underlying unencrypted volume, exposing data at rest in the snapshot as well.
The security group allows inbound SSH (port 22) from 0.0.0.0/0, exposing administrative access to the entire internet.

The security group allows inbound HTTP (port 80) from 0.0.0.0/0. While this may be intended for a web server, combined with the lack of any additional restriction it broadens the attack surface unnecessarily beyond required sources.
The security group allows all outbound traffic (all ports/protocols) to 0.0.0.0/0, providing a potential data exfiltration path and no egress control (Zero Trust violation).
The subnet has map_public_ip_on_launch set to true, causing instances launched here to automatically receive public IP addresses, expanding external exposure.
The subnet has map_public_ip_on_launch set to true, causing instances launched here to automatically receive public IP addresses, expanding external exposure.
The S3 bucket storing VPC flow logs has no server-side encryption configuration, leaving sensitive network traffic logs stored unencrypted.

findings.issue_category: missing access controls / public access block
findings.description: The S3 bucket has no public access block or bucket policy restricting access, and force_destroy is enabled, risking accidental public exposure or data loss of flow log data.
